title: Police raid in Shreveport
summary: Police burst into the Shreveport rooming house with the Dunbar orchestra and beat everyone with billy clubs; his thoughts on change in Jackson.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Back to Louisiana again, over in Shreveport, Louisiana. I remember I was over there with the Don Dunbar Orchestra. And some kids in the neighborhood were studying music, and they heard about this young kid playing, so they came over, and we fooled around, blowing the horns, one evening I imagine at about 9:30. And we were living in this big rooming house, 450 Oakland Avenue -- I'll never forget it. And there was a White family that lived next door. And evidently, they called the police and said we were disturbing the peace or something. And I'm upstairs with the kids, and the rest of... A lot of the guys in the band were downstairs, playing cards with some of the ladies that lived there, you know. And the police just came in, didn't ask any questions -- and they just started whuppin' heads.
You know, just whuppin' the guys in the band, and the girls -- everybody. Just started swingin' their billy-clubs.

That's the kind of stuff they used to do down there! It could get pretty wild, with that racial thing down there during those days. They tell me it's much, much better now in general -- in general, you know. Even in Jackson, my people tell me... In fact, my Aunt's husband owned The Jackson Advocate, the Black newspaper there before he passed, and she runs it now... But he used to try to get me to come back home. I'll go there when I can get around to it. But he used to tell me, "Come back, because people want to see you, people want to know you." And then he said, "You'd be surprised. There are White people that know about you that want to meet you and want to see you," you know. So evidently, they are making some different changes down there now, you know.
